title: SYSK Selects: How Aphrodisiacs Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on aphrodisiacs (originally aired March 2009 per the intro). The hosts open with a cold-open on Spanish fly (a beetle-derived substance, dangerous, not a true aphrodisiac), then define aphrodisiacs as substances that stimulate sexual desire, distinguishing them from performance enhancers like Viagra. They explain the physiology of sexual arousal (limbic system, blood flow, neurotransmitters), note the FDA recognizes no aphrodisiac, and discuss testosterone and estrogen's roles. Historical lore follows: Persian honey and the origin of "honeymoon," Roman oysters, avocados, and phallic-shaped foods, and the eating of animal sex organs. They cover ginseng (jensing), chocolate and its compounds, the Aztec ruler Montezuma's chocolate consumption, and smell (Dr. Alan Hirsch's penile blood-flow study with odors such as pumpkin pie, buttered popcorn, and cucumber), pheromones and the vomeronasal organ, a twin pheromone bar anecdote, and placebo effects. The episode closes with listener limericks and an email address.

segments.title: Opening banter and Spanish fly
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode on aphrodisiacs and the hosts banter. They discuss Spanish fly, which is a beetle, not a fly, and its dangers.

segments.title: Defining aphrodisiacs and sexual arousal
segments.summary: The hosts define aphrodisiacs as substances that stimulate sexual desire, distinguishing them from performance enhancers like Viagra. They explain the physiology of arousal, including limbic system activation, blood flow to the pelvic area, and neurotransmitters.

segments.title: FDA stance and testosterone
segments.summary: The FDA recognizes no compound as an aphrodisiac, since libido is hard to define and study. The hosts discuss testosterone's link to arousal in men and a 2000 University of Utrecht study on sublingual testosterone in women with low libido.

segments.title: Ancient Persia, honey and the honeymoon
segments.summary: The Persians reportedly believed honey was an aphrodisiac, and newlyweds drank honey for a month, giving rise to the word honeymoon. Ancient Rome is also noted for its aphrodisiac beliefs.

segments.title: Oysters, avocados and phallic foods
segments.summary: Oysters top aphrodisiac lists, due to zinc and iron content. Avocados, figs, bananas and other foods are considered aphrodisiacs because they resemble sex organs. Some cultures ate animal sex organs.

segments.title: Ginseng and chocolate
segments.summary: Ginseng (jensing) has been shown in one study to improve erectile function scores in men. Chocolate contains phenylethylamine and serotonin. The hosts recall Montezuma drinking large amounts of chocolate.

segments.title: Smell and Alan Hirsch's study
segments.summary: Dr. Alan Hirsch of the Smell and Taste Treatment and Research Center studied how odors affected penile blood flow in men; cheese pizza, buttered popcorn, lavender and pumpkin pie were tested. A combination of odors was found most arousing to women.

segments.title: Pheromones and placebo
segments.summary: The hosts discuss pheromones in animals and humans, the vomeronasal organ, an informal twin study in a bar where the pheromone-treated twin was approached more, and the possibility that aphrodisiacs work as placebos.

segments.title: Listener limericks and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener limericks from Ryan of Victoria, British Columbia, and Brendan Franklin of Tucson, Arizona are read. The hosts invite listeners to send email to the show.
